documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Milking exposes women dairy farmers to sustained trunk flexion and repetitive upper-limb loading, producing a high burden of musculoskeletal disorders. Ergonomics education is the conventional preventive strategy, but added benefit from structured exercise is untested in this population. Methods: In this assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial, 50 women who had milked cows for ≥5 years were allocated to ergonomics training alone (control, n = 25) or ergonomics training plus a 12-week, home-based, equipment-free exercise programme (experimental, n = 25). The primary outcome was pain intensity (NRS), designated as primary only after data collection, so all analyses are exploratory; secondary outcomes were musculoskeletal symptoms (Nordic Questionnaire, seven-day recall at both assessments), upper-limb function (QuickDASH), depression (BDI) and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). Continuous outcomes were analysed by mixed-model ANOVA and ANCOVA. Results: All participants completed the trial, with self-reported exercise adherence of 100%. Time × group interactions favoured the combined intervention for pain (F1,48 = 55.19, p < 0.001; baseline-adjusted mean difference −1.25, 95% CI −1.58 to −0.92), upper-limb function, depressive symptom scores and three WHOQOL-BREF domains (all p < 0.05), but not social relationships (p = 0.896). Mean NRS reduction was −3.76 ± 0.66 versus −2.24 ± 0.78 (d = −2.10), and symptomatic body regions fell by −2.64 ± 0.70 versus −1.20 ± 1.53 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Both groups improved, and adding a 12-week equipment-free exercise programme was associated with greater short-term, self-reported gains. These exploratory findings from a small single-region sample need confirmation in larger trials with objective adherence measures and longer follow-up.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The growing prevalence of chronic wound infections presents a major global healthcare challenge due to delayed healing, prolonged hospitalization, and increased rates of limb amputation. Conventional diagnostic approaches, including clinical assessment, microbiological culture, and laboratory-based analyses, are often limited by subjective interpretation, delayed turnaround times, invasive sampling, and an inability to continuously monitor the dynamic wound microenvironment. Because wound infection involves changes in both host physiology and microbial activity, reliance on a single biomarker may not adequately characterize wound status, highlighting the potential of multimodal point-of-care diagnostic platforms. Recent advances in wearable biosensors, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), nanomaterials, and artificial intelligence (AI) have supported the development of multimodal approaches for monitoring complementary host- and pathogen-derived biomarkers to facilitate rapid, non-invasive, and continuous wound infection assessment. This review examines selected multimodal biosensing approaches for wound infection detection, with a focus on electrochemical biosensors, SERS, and AI-assisted data analytics within point-of-care diagnostic frameworks. The review discusses (1) key wound infection biomarkers and the fundamental principles of electrochemical and SERS-based sensing; (2) recent developments in multimodal biosensing platforms, advanced plasmonic materials, and AI-assisted data interpretation and multimodal data fusion; and (3) current challenges and future opportunities for the clinical translation of point-of-care wound diagnostics. By combining complementary sensing modalities with AI-driven data analytics, these approaches may support earlier infection detection, continuous non-invasive monitoring, personalized wound management, and more informed clinical decision-making.

Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.

Abstract Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities for English language teaching through personalized learning, interactive practice, automated feedback, and instructional material development. However, its effective integration requires pedagogical planning, digital competence, and attention to ethical considerations. These issues are particularly relevant to English language education in Uzbekistan, where teachers work in diverse educational settings.

Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) has become a key benchmark for evaluating natural language processing systems, and multiple-choice question answering is widely adopted for assessing reasoning, comprehension, and commonsense inference capabilities. However, traditional embedding-based retrieval models often struggle with complex reasoning and lack sufficient external knowledge. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong language understanding and reasoning abilities, relying on a single model remains challenging due to hallucinations, model biases, and differences in training data, architectures, and domain expertise. As a result, no individual model can consistently achieve optimal performance across diverse multiple-choice question answering tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an ensemble framework for multiple-choice question answering. The framework incorporates a novel model selection mechanism that identifies model combinations with minimal error overlap, thereby maximizing error-correction capability. In addition, when disagreements occur among base models, a Thinking Model is dynamically invoked to analyze and resolve conflicting predictions, enabling advanced reasoning only when necessary. Experimental results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms individual models across multiple datasets and previous ensemble approaches. At the same time, it significantly reduces inference time and computational cost compared to the strongest benchmark models.

BackgroundChiselling involves repetitive, precision work with constrained postures and high hand loads, contributing to upper-limb musculoskeletal disorders among artisans. Despite extensive work on workstation ergonomics and general hand-tool design, few studies have systematically translated ergonomic risk-assessment findings into specific chisel-handle design requirements and evaluated the resulting intervention in a real craft-sector setting.ObjectiveThis study aimed to characterize ergonomic exposures in chiselling, translate these findings to concrete handle design requirements, and evaluate a prototype handle's short-term usability versus conventional handles.MethodsFifty male artisans underwent NMQ, palm pain mapping, RULA and ART assessment. Risk findings informed a modular ergonomic handle (elliptical contour, 25-40 mm diameter, 10-15° cant, strike ferrule). A counterbalanced in-lab within-subject short-term usability comparison (n = 30) was conducted alongside post-trial acute hand pain mapping and targeted ART posture sub-component reassessment.ResultsA high prevalence of upper-limb musculoskeletal symptoms and dominant-hand biomechanical risk were identified. The prototype was strongly preferred and rated easier and more comfortable to use, and it markedly reduced acute pain at the thumb base and first finger-web. Usability improved across all items and acute thenar/first-web pain fell substantially (Zones 19-20, paired d > 2.9), with parallel reductions in the wrist-posture and force-demand sub-components of the ART assessment.ConclusionsRisk-informed handle redesign yielded immediate, objectively corroborated hand-level benefits. The study contributes a low-cost, retrofittable ergonomic chisel handle and replicable risk-to-design pathway applicable to woodworking artisans and similar occupations. Longitudinal field validation is necessary to establish sustained reductions in musculoskeletal disorder prevalence and productivity gains.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Smartphone use has become integral to university students’ academic and social activities, but prolonged use combined with non-ergonomic wrist positions and body postures may increase biomechanical strain and contribute to wrist pain. This study examined ergonomic risk factors associated with wrist pain among smartphone-using university students. Methods: A quantitative observational cross-sectional study was conducted from June to July 2026 among undergraduate Public Health students at Universitas Tamalatea Makassar. A total of 78 students were recruited using accidental sampling from a population of 336 students. Smartphone use, wrist position, and body posture were assessed using an ergonomics-based questionnaire referring to Rapid Upper Limb Assessment principles, while wrist pain was measured using the Numeric Rating Scale. Associations were analyzed using Pearson’s Chi-square test, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) estimated from the 2×2 contingency tables. Results: Wrist pain was reported by 64 students (82.1%). High smartphone use was associated with greater odds of wrist pain than low use (OR=3.44; 95% CI: 1.03–11.51; p=0.038). A non-ergonomic wrist position showed the strongest association with wrist pain (OR=10.14; 95% CI: 2.52–40.78; p<0.001). Non-ergonomic body posture was also significantly associated with wrist pain (OR=4.77; 95% CI: 1.34–16.98; p=0.011). Conclusion: Smartphone-related ergonomic exposures were significantly associated with wrist pain among university students, particularly non-neutral wrist positioning. Campus-based ergonomic education should emphasize neutral wrist alignment, appropriate posture, reduced prolonged smartphone use, and regular rest breaks to minimize musculoskeletal strain.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a tool for sustainable development, yet the ethical costs of this role remain scattered across separate bodies of literature. This systematic review aims to identify the ethical issues arising at the intersection of AI, ethics, and sustainability. Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2020 statement, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in February 2026, yielding 5,794 records. Screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal were carried out by two researchers, and 74 studies were included. Verbatim passages addressing the intersection were extracted from each study and examined using a hybrid thematic approach, resulting in 921 coded passages. Five themes were identified: algorithmic bias and unequal AI outcomes; privacy, surveillance, and human autonomy; transparency, accountability, and epistemic integrity; AI governance and corporate responsibility; and the ecological ethics of AI systems. Concerns regarding transparency and accountability accounted for the largest share of passages (30.9%), while ecological concerns were voiced across all five themes rather than in a separate discussion. The themes were mapped onto the environmental, social, and governance dimensions of sustainability and onto the United Nations sustainable development goals. Transparency and accountability thus emerge as a structural prerequisite rather than a procedural add-on for sustainable AI. Educational research is markedly underrepresented at this intersection (5 of 74 studies); the implications of the five themes for science, mathematics, and technology education are therefore developed in detail, from carbon- and water-footprint modelling tasks to data-justice and AI-literacy work in the classroom.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from speculative theory to a transformative global technology with insightful ethical, social, and legal implications. In Muslim contexts, the framework of maqāṣid al-sharīʿah - the higher objectives of Islamic law - offers a rich, value-oriented approach to evaluating and guiding the development of AI. It highlights both opportunities and risks across key domains such as healthcare, online content moderation, surveillance, and economic displacement. Acknowledging that AI has emerged as one of the most unsettling technologies of the twenty-first century with its attendant global transformative capacity, its implications for societies like Nigeria, where religious, cultural, and ethical frameworks shape governance and social order, remain underexplored. This article examines the revolution of AI in Nigeria through the lens of Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah (the higher objectives of Islamic law). Drawing on classical Islamic jurisprudence and contemporary AI debates, the study analyzes how AI aligns with or threatens the preservation of religion (ḥifẓ al-dīn), life (ḥifẓ al-nafs), intellect (ḥifẓ al-ʿaql), lineage (ḥifẓ al-nasl), and property (ḥifẓ al-māl). It argues that Nigeria’s engagement with AI must not only reflect global ethical principles but also incorporate indigenous religious traditions to ensure justice, human dignity, and social welfare. The article concludes with maqāṣid-based policy recommendations to guide Nigeria’s AI future.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Forecasting the direction and magnitude of stock price movements remains one of the most persistently difficult problems in applied machine learning, owing to the noisy, non-stationary, and weak-form-efficient character of financial time series. This survey examines three recent studies that approach the problem through complementary lenses: an explainable Decision Tree that builds dynamic, industry-specific lexicons from financial news to classify next-day price-change magnitude [1]; a feature-engineering and portfolio-construction pipeline that derives new price-based predictors via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and a proposed Statistical Average Method (SAM) before applying eight regression architectures, including Bi-LSTM [2]; and an LSTM-based trend classifier that fuses FinBERT-scored Twitter sentiment with price data to forecast North American and European bank-stock movements during the macroeconomically turbulent year of 2022 [3]. Beyond summarising each study's objectives, methodology, data, and results, this survey situates the three works within the broader and rapidly evolving literature on deep sequence models (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, and transformer architectures), sentiment analysis with pretrained financial language models such as FinBERT, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in finance. A structured comparative analysis contrasts the three studies along ten dimensions, including data sources, feature engineering, model architecture, explainability, validation design, and reported performance, while explicitly cautioning against directly ranking studies whose prediction tasks and evaluation metrics are not commensurable. A cross-domain case study of an attention-based legislative-vote predictor is retained to examine whether a learned similarity mechanism could improve on the fixed similarity rules used throughout the finance literature reviewed here. The survey's contribution lies in bringing explainable lexicon-based methods, statistically engineered price features, and sentiment-driven deep learning together within a single comparative framework, and in using that synthesis to identify concrete, evidence-grounded gaps around auxiliary-signal fusion, the explainability of high-accuracy sequence models, and cross-market generalisation.

Abstract Recent developments of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) are transforming several sectors like Industry 4.0, smart cities, intelligent healthcare, and smart transportation. The AIoT can be employed in urban mobility to enable real-time monitoring and intelligent decision-making in the transportation sector. Traffic congestion classification is a significant aspect of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as the rising urban population has contributed to severe congestion complexity that impacts air quality, road safety, and travel time. Accurate classification of congestion patterns improves traffic management and mitigates environmental impacts. Although precisely predicting congestion spread is still problematic, owing to the complex, non-linear, and dynamic nature of traffic patterns. As deep learning advances, efficient models are required to address the challenges in smart urban mobility systems. Therefore, this study presents a Deep Learning-Based Urban Mobility Intelligent System for Traffic Congestion Framework (DLUMIS-TCF). The proposed DLUMIS-TCF model analyzes urban mobility data with trip-level records for precise traffic congestion level classification. The preprocessing stage includes missing value handling, outlier detection, feature scaling, temporal attribute extraction, and spatial coordinate utilization to prepare the data for effective learning. For feature selection, the model utilizes Elastic Net to select the relevant spatio-temporal features from the dataset. In addition, the traffic congestion level classification is performed using a heterogeneous spatiotemporal graph attention network. Furthermore, the optimization of the model is carried out using the AdaBelief optimizer to improve convergence and performance. To improve the interpretability of the model, SHAP is used to explain the contribution of input features toward the classification results. To assess the performance of the proposed DLUMIS-TCF model, experiments are carried out on an Urban Mobility Intelligence Dataset obtained from the Kaggle repository. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed model in predicting traffic congestion compared to other methods. Thus, the proposed DLUMIS-TCF approach can be useful for urban traffic management, congestion control, and intelligent transportation systems.

Background: Precision laboratory diagnosis increasingly relies on the interpretation of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. Conventional workflows tend to examine biomarkers, molecular measurements, immunological findings, and clinical characteristics along partly separate analytical pathways. Artificial intelligence (AI) can uncover complex relationships in high-dimensional biomedical data, yet many such systems remain hard to interpret at the point of clinical use. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) renders algorithmic outputs more transparent by identifying the features, modalities, and interactions that shape a prediction. Objective: This manuscript proposes an explainable multimodal AI framework for precision laboratory diagnosis, termed XMAI-PLD, which unites conventional laboratory biomarkers, molecular profiles, immunological signatures, and clinical data within a single analytical architecture. The framework is designed to support, rather than supplant, laboratory expertise and clinical judgement. Framework: The architecture comprises seven interconnected layers: data acquisition; quality control and harmonisation; modality-specific representation; multimodal fusion; diagnostic inference; explainability and uncertainty assessment; and laboratory–clinical decision support. Biomarker measurements contribute quantitative biochemical information, molecular profiles characterise genomic or molecular alterations, immunological signatures capture host-response patterns, and clinical variables supply patient-level context. Each stream is processed separately before being integrated through multimodal learning, and explanations are generated at the modality and feature levels to reveal the principal drivers of each output. Clinical and Laboratory Relevance: The framework addresses the shortcomings of isolated single-modality models, namely incomplete biological representation, heterogeneous data structures, missing information, analytical variability, and limited interpretability. Its proposed outputs comprise diagnostic probabilities, contributing features, modality-level evidence, uncertainty estimates, and cases flagged for human review. Particular emphasis falls on analytical validity, calibration, external validation, data provenance, subgroup assessment, cybersecurity, privacy, and human oversight. Conclusion: Explainable multimodal AI offers a promising route towards a more integrated diagnostic representation of laboratory and clinical evidence. Its worth will hinge not only on predictive performance but also on analytical robustness, reproducibility, interpretability, calibration, clinical usefulness, and sustained human oversight. Prospective, multicentre evaluation is required before such systems enter routine diagnostic practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to explain FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) symptoms based on maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness, with a particular focus on the mediating role of artificial intelligence dependency among female high school adolescents. Methods and Materials: This correlational study employed a structural equation modeling approach to investigate the relationships among maladaptive perfectionism, emotional loneliness, artificial intelligence dependency, and FOMO symptoms. The statistical population consisted of all female students enrolled in secondary high schools in Dezful, Iran, during the 2025–2026 academic year. A total of 250 students were selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Fear of Missing Out Scale developed by Przybylski et al. (2013), the Multidimensional Perfectionism Questionnaire by Hewitt and Flett (2004), the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale by DiTommaso et al. (2004), and the Artificial Intelligence Dependency Questionnaire developed by Huang et al. (2024). Data analysis was conducted using descriptive and inferential statistics in SPSS and AMOS software packages. Path analysis and structural equation modeling were utilized to evaluate both direct and indirect relationships among the study variables and to assess the overall model fit. Findings: The results demonstrated that maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness significantly predicted FOMO symptoms both directly and indirectly through artificial intelligence dependency. Maladaptive perfectionism showed a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.411, p < .01), while emotional loneliness also exhibited a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.506, p < .01). Furthermore, maladaptive perfectionism had a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.267, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect through artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.124, p < .01). Similarly, emotional loneliness exerted a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.259, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect mediated by artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.152, p < .01). Artificial intelligence dependency itself significantly and positively predicted FOMO symptoms (β = 0.301, p < .01). Model fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the proposed structural model to the observed data. Conclusion: The findings suggest that adolescents with higher levels of maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness are more likely to develop dependency on artificial intelligence technologies, which in turn intensifies FOMO symptoms. Artificial intelligence dependency functions as a significant psychological mechanism linking individual vulnerabilities and social-emotional difficulties to heightened fear of missing out. These results highlight the importance of addressing maladaptive perfectionistic standards, strengthening real-world emotional relationships, and promoting healthy patterns of AI use in interventions designed to reduce FOMO among adolescents.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

BackgroundThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the clinical work of rehabilitation therapists in post stroke rehabilitation has the potential to transform their work performance, habits, and routines. The impact could potentially enhance integration of assessment/data analysis, personalizing therapies, documentation, and promoting home program adherence.ObjectiveThis study assesses occupational and physical therapists' current perspectives on AI/ML in post-stroke clinical rehabilitation and examines perceived barriers to potential application of AI/ML in their clinical work.MethodsThis mixed methods study includes quantitative survey data collected pre/post an AI/ML educational webinar, as well as qualitative focus group analysis that includes therapist attitudes and experiences with AI/ML, practical applications to using AI/ML, as well as the difficulties associated. The recruited therapists include occupational and physical therapy practitioners from the United States and Asia. Individuals included in the study had to have a caseload of 30% persons with stroke.ResultsFour key themes emerged from qualitative analysis: 1) current clinical work practice and identified gaps, 2) current therapists' perceptions of AI/ML, 3) perceived future of AI/ML in clinical work practices and 4) steps needed for implementation. Survey data reporting frequencies of technology use and AI/ML perceptions are integrated into qualitative findings.ConclusionsTherapists can articulate potential future uses for AI/ML technology in post-stroke rehabilitation, however, remain uncertain about when, how, and at what cost utilization will be supported in clinical work environments. Therapists desire education and support to utilize the evolving technologies in practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.

Purpose This paper examines the ethical and epistemological implications of language generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lenses of speech act theory, conversational implicature and second-order cybernetics. LLMs are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs actively participate in shaping discourse in ways that carry consequences for meaning, responsibility and pluralism. Design/methodology/approach The paper introduces the concept of soft derogation to describe a form of linguistic exclusion, one that operates through euphemization, omission and the simulation of neutrality rather than overt offense. Such processes can subtly promote or suppress certain ideas, values or identities without transparent authorship or intention. The result is a shift toward an algorithmically generated form of newspeak, where expressive possibilities are narrowed through alignment protocols and safety layers. Findings Drawing on second-order cybernetics, the paper argues that ethical responsibility for AI-generated language is distributed across developers, deployers, institutional stakeholders and human interpreters. While users co-construct meaning within recursive socio-technical systems, the upstream actors who design alignment protocols, moderation layers and deployment conditions bear primary responsibility for the communicative environments they create. Originality/value Relatively little work has examined how the pertinent philosophical frameworks can illuminate forms of linguistic influence that operate through euphemization, omission and simulated neutrality. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how algorithmically generated language can shape discourse while appearing neutral.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Foundation models are extending research on financial fraud and financial crime from isolated risk detection to document understanding, relational analysis, and investigative workflows. A gap nevertheless separates model outputs from candidate evidence and actionable conclusions. This survey examines advances in six families of foundation models: language, vision, speech, temporal, graph, and tabular models. It compares their roles and limitations along two dimensions: the risk-control lifecycle and the directness of the supporting evidence. Existing studies show that pretraining can support representation reuse and the processing of unstructured information, with direct validation in some financial tasks. Cross-modal identity binding, information availability over time, report faithfulness, and case-level benefits require separate evaluation. Evidence on investigative agents spans prototypes, controlled tasks, expert assessments, and industry disclosures, which establish different aspects of workflow feasibility, task performance, and user assessment. Establishing gains in investigative efficiency and reductions in financial losses requires case-level comparative evidence. We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption transformed work structures after 2022, raising psychological safety concerns as efficiency priorities overshadow human-centered employee wellbeing. Objective This longitudinal study investigates how engagement is framed as a corporate communication strategy in Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 technology firms during early large-scale AI adoption (2022–2024). Methods Using IRaMuTeQ, 150 S&P 500 corporate reports (2022–2024) underwent Reinert's Descending Hierarchical Classification, Correspondence Factorial Analysis, and similarity network analysis, employing chi-square ( χ 2 ) marker filtering. Results Findings reveal a three-stage trajectory mapping onto dynamic capabilities: initial sensing (2022), platform seizing (2023), and process transformation (2024). However, human-centered engagement language (meaningfulness, safety, vigor) remained structurally marginalized, failing to form a stable lexical cluster and framing participation strictly through technical integration. Conclusions Public discourse serves as a proxy for enacting dynamic capabilities. Practically, HR leaders should prospectively audit AI communications to ensure technical efficiency narratives do not displace human-centered and psychological safety registers.

Artificial intelligence requires systematic reflection on the relationship between technological progress, collective responsibility and the dignity of the person, making a new social pact necessary. The article links dependence on fossil fuels to geopolitical imbalances, inflationary pressures and the ability of authoritarian regimes to support power policies, proposing international coordination, including at the UN, that reconciles energy security, climate protection and the transition to renewable sources and, in perspective, nuclear fusion. This analysis is accompanied by the criticism of an economy based exclusively on solvency, which excludes needs without adequate purchasing power from the production and distribution of essential goods. To combat poverty, inequality and vulnerability to war, an international agency capable of promoting socially useful work and coordinating the production and distribution of fundamental resources is envisaged. In this framework, artificial intelligence and robotics could contribute to the analysis of needs, the organization of work, agriculture, assistance and scientific research, as long as they remain subordinate to democratic decision-making and criteria of transparency, human control and non-discrimination. Finally, the technological comparison between the United States, China and Europe shows the need, especially for Europe, to strengthen investment, research and regulatory capacity. Energy, peace, social justice and innovation are thus brought back to the different dimensions of a single pact based on collective responsibility and human dignity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Whether a new technology needs its own law is an old question, and for artificial intelligence (AI), it has been posed at the wrong level of abstraction. Both the case against technology-specific law and the case for regulation by design treat the AI model as the regulated object, although a general-purpose model acquires its risk only when deployed. This article relocates the regulatory object to the deployment workflow, defined as the envelope of thresholds, escalation pathways and human checkpoints that surrounds a model in use, and reads the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as management-based regulation that works only where the workflow is specifiable and a standing supervisor examines it. Hungary’s first-wave implementation shows the second condition deciding the outcome: the same obligations are supervised by the central bank in finance and by a ministry with no examination relationship in employment, so the Act’s uniform text conceals uneven supervision within one Member State. The Digital Omnibus on AI, which postpones the high-risk obligations because standards and authorities are late, opens a window to build supervision deliberately: the priority is not better definitions but better supervision.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents record in their trajectories which strategies failed and how they recovered, yet an agent that resolves a problem in one episode may repeat the same diagnostic detour in the next. Work on reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition addresses this gap under different names, making methods and their gains hard to compare. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task-execution trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies; it may be a trajectory kept as a precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We review methods through four lifecycle functions: formation selects or derives candidate experience from trajectories, organization makes it accessible, utilization applies it to current decisions or internalizes it into model parameters, and maintenance admits, consolidates, revises, and retires it as evidence accumulates. A recurring source of failure is guidance that loses its link to its applicability conditions and supporting evidence: it is over-generalized during formation, misapplied during utilization, and left unrevised during maintenance. We organize evaluation around intrinsic experience quality, the experience utilization process, and downstream effects, and separate three improvement claims: fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism. The reviewed studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Across seven application settings, we derive recommendations on whether reuse justifies its cost, what to retain, how strongly experience should influence a task, and when to revise it. We close with eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to correcting propagated errors and testing whether gains accumulate.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) weakens a practical assumption in the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS): that estimated student workload remains a credible proxy for learning when assessment evidence is interpretable. This conceptual article examines what follows when academic products are routinely produced through hybrid human–AI cognition. Drawing on Kane’s interpretation/use argument, assessment-security scholarship and recent work on GenAI in higher education, it reconstructs ECTS as an inferential system in which scores, generalisation, extrapolation and credit-awarding uses must all be warranted. The analysis shows that opaque take-home production can weaken each link: scoring may misread distributed authorship, generalisation becomes unstable, extrapolation to learning outcomes is less secure, and credit awards risk retaining administrative form without evidential force. The article proposes verified learning as a credit-level validity condition and specifies four safeguards: programme-level alignment, authentic transfer tasks, process visibility with declared AI use, and strategic controlled verification. It also identifies equity and governance conditions required for these safeguards to support, rather than undermine, comparability across ECTS-based institutions in AI-rich assessment environments. The contribution is to connect task-level assessment validity to credit legitimacy and to translate that connection into practical design and quality-assurance implications for European higher education policy.

Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming the nature of work, employee roles and human resource management practices across organisations. Deposit Money Banks are particularly affected because their operations involve extensive information processing, customer interaction, documentation, decision support and knowledge-intensive activities. However, the extent to which Generative AI contributes to employee productivity may depend on how effectively organisations manage workforce transformation. This study examined the relationship between Generative AI and workforce transformation and proposed an AI-HRM framework for improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State. The study specifically examined the relationships between Generative AI and employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and employee productivity. A cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of selected Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State using a structured questionnaire. Reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. Out of 344 questionnaire administered, 300 usable copies were retrieved and use for the analysis with the aid of SPSS version 27.0. The findings suggest that Generative AI should not be viewed merely as a replacement for human labour but as a technology capable of augmenting employees’ capabilities and transforming the way work is organised and performed. The study therefore proposed an AI-HRM framework based on AI readiness, Generative AI adoption, employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and productivity improvement. The study concludes that Deposit Money Banks can achieve greater productivity benefits from Generative AI when its adoption is supported by appropriate HRM practices, continuous employee development and effective human–AI collaboration. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a context-specific AI-HRM framework for managing workforce transformation and improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but its educational value depends on how it is used. This conceptual article examines ways in which future teachers can use AI to ask questions, compare explanations, and check evidence rather than accept ready-made answers. A focused review of work on critical thinking, media literacy, and AI in education was used to build a practical teaching sequence. The analysis suggests that AI can support discussion and reflection when students first form their own view, check external sources, and explain their final decision. The article also describes risks such as confident errors and overreliance. The proposed sequence is a design recommendation, not a tested intervention.

Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.

Data-driven decision-making increasingly depends on long socio-technical chains in which data is collected, integrated, modelled, ranked and circulated before it reaches a decision-maker. Existing governance instruments focus mainly on safety, rights and compliance, and existing scholarship treats data governance, platform power, algorithmic governance and information integrity as separate problems. As a result, the reliability and legitimacy of the knowledge on which decisions rest — their epistemic quality — remains largely ungoverned. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. Using an integrative literature review and a model-type conceptual design, it synthesises datafication theory, platform capitalism, algorithmic governance and social epistemology into a single data-to-decision lens. It contributes (i) a taxonomy of thirteen epistemic risks located along the data-to-decision lifecycle; (ii) the Epistemic Risk Governance Framework (ERGF), which maps four governance pillars onto six actionable governance dimensions; (iii) seven testable propositions, including a weakest-link principle of epistemic governance; and (iv) a comparative analysis showing where the ERGF extends the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the UNESCO Recommendation and Kenya’s emerging data and AI governance instruments. The framework is illustrated through Kenyan decision contexts and accompanied by a design science agenda for its empirical evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study undertook an experimental comparison of visual acquisition for the avoidance of Mid-Air Collisions (MAC) when using cueing provided by Head-Up Display (HUD) and Helmet-Mounted Display (HMD) symbology. BACKGROUND: Previous work has shown that providing accurate cueing can improve visual detection performance, but no study had quantified the impact of providing cues via a HMD to reduce MAC risk. METHOD: Military fast jet pilots flew two scenarios in a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation. In one, a HUD provided cues to nearby aircraft. In the other, a HMD was used alongside the HUD to provide cues. The study measured visual acquisition range of aircraft that posed a MAC risk, as well as subjective workload, Situation Awareness (SA), gaze direction, and qualitative feedback. RESULTS: Visual acquisition occurred at a longer range when HMD cues were available compared to using a HUD only. HMD cueing was associated with lower subjective workload and higher perceived SA. Participant gaze direction indicated that HMD cues resulted in a more focused visual search. CONCLUSION: Including HMD alongside the existing HUD used in military aircraft improved visual acquisition of MAC hazards, beyond that offered by HUD alone. The clear presentation of spatially referenced cues in the HMD enabled pilots to use a focused visual search process, improved SA and reduced workload.

The Question Everyone Is Forgetting OpenAI's release of more than 700 mathematical manuscripts has provoked an extraordinary question: is this the final nail in the coffin? Are mathematicians no longer needed? Mathematicians, and indeed the world, are so busy debating whether mathematicians will remain relevant now that artificial intelligence can apparently solve some of mathematics' hardest problems that everyone is overlooking a much more fundamental question: Who conceived those problems in the first place? Who decided that these were the questions worth asking? Understanding this is, I believe, the most essential part of the entire debate. The question is not who can perform the greatest number of successful mathematical operations. It is who gave mathematics its problems, and what is lost when the development of an answer is treated as disposable. I am concerned with the distinction between the final theorem, the proof establishing it, and the intellectual journeys through which new questions appear before that theorem has been reached. We celebrate the mathematician who solves a difficult problem. We award prizes for proofs, commemorate breakthroughs, and measure mathematical progress by the number and significance of problems resolved. But before any of these achievements became possible, someone had to conceive the question. Before a theorem could be proved, someone had to recognize that there was something worth proving. Before an equation could be solved, someone had to recognize that a relationship required mathematical expression. And before a field of mathematics could exist, human beings had to develop the intellectual appetite, intuition, and conceptual language that made its questions conceivable. This is not a minor preliminary step. It is the foundational act of mathematical creation. Consider the Navier–Stokes problem. Its mathematical formulation emerged from humanity's investigation of fluids, motion, physical forces, and the behavior of matter. The equations were not waiting in a computer as an arbitrary collection of symbols. They arose from human beings observing the world, attempting to understand it, and translating that encounter into mathematics. The same is true, in different ways, of the questions that gave rise to geometry, calculus, probability, topology, number theory, and the countless mathematical structures that followed. Even when mathematics eventually becomes so abstract that its connection to ordinary experience is almost impossible to recognize, its intellectual ancestry remains human. This matters precisely because we may be entering an era in which an AI system can deliver a proposed proof faster than a mathematical community can assimilate it. If we measure mathematical progress only by the answers delivered, the most consequential losses may escape our measurement altogether. The important question is therefore not simply whether AI can solve the Riemann hypothesis, the Navier–Stokes problem, or hundreds of other conjectures. It is whether solving questions conceived within the human mathematical enterprise is equivalent to possessing the intelligence, intuition, and origins of thought that created that enterprise. I argue that it is not. Solving a problem and being the kind of intelligence from which the problem was born are two fundamentally different accomplishments.

Mining environments are extreme subsurface ecosystems characterized by elevated concentrations of metals and minerals, limited light, and high particulate loads. Occupational health research in mining has traditionally emphasized physical and chemical hazards, whereas biological exposures remain less well-characterized. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on mining-associated microbial communities, bioaerosols, occupational exposure, respiratory health, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The literature search covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception through August 2026. Evidence from coal, uranium, metal mining, acid mine drainage, and mine dust environments indicates that geochemical conditions and mining activities shape microbial communities. Drilling, blasting, excavation, and ore transport can aerosolize microbial cells, spores, and dust-associated microbial components, creating plausible inhalation pathways. Metal-rich environments may also favor persistence and co-selection of metal- and antibiotic-resistance determinants within environmental microbial communities. Metagenomic sequencing and environmental DNA approaches have expanded detection of microbial diversity, functional genes, and environmental resistomes. However, environmental detection does not establish microbial viability, effective worker exposure, transmission, or disease causation. Future research should integrate standardized environmental and personal microbial exposure measurements with respirable dust and chemical monitoring, longitudinal occupational epidemiology, and functional validation of resistance determinants to determine the actual occupational-health significance of mining-associated microbiomes.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

BackgroundEducational videos play a crucial role in enhancing healthcare delivery. Developing an educational video designed to improve patient understanding of catastrophic treatment. During the video's creation, two voiceover methods were employed: human voices and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated voices. To date, the impact of voice-over origin-whether human or AI-on patient knowledge acquisition remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study aimed to assess the differences in knowledge and practice scores among cancer patients exposed to educational video materials about chemotherapy, comparing human voice with AI-generated voice narrations.MethodsA total of 129 cancer patients participated in this study. Designed as a case-control study, participants were divided into three groups: a control group, a group receiving videos with human voice narrations, and a group receiving videos with AI-generated voice narrations. All participants completed a questionnaire assessing their understanding of chemotherapy. A three-group quantitative comparative analysis was conducted, focusing on topics such as administration procedures, treatment goals, and the management of adverse drug reactions.Key findingsBoth educational videos with human- and AI-generated voiceovers should be incorporated into the oncology healthcare system due to their effectiveness in improving understanding of treatment. Notably, educational videos featuring human-voice narration consistently enrich knowledge and attitude scores among cancer patients across all assessed chemotherapy topics.ConclusionThe educational videos, whether in human or AI voices, were effective in increasing cancer patients' knowledge and attitudes across all key topics. There was a sustained trend toward human-voice videos in knowledge and attitudes among cancer patients; therefore, the human educational video showed significant improvement in understanding of chemotherapy administration, goals, and adverse drug reactions. Although there was no difference between human and AI voice education, trends toward combining human voice with realistic scenario videos should be considered to facilitate deeper patient understanding.

This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
