documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, is transforming computer-assisted learning and teaching in higher education. This study investigates how ChatGPT can support learning by reducing cognitive load, with particular emphasis on the roles of user technological confidence and affective trust in artificial intelligence within the framework of Cognitive Load Theory. The study employs quantitative analysis based on data from 12,085 respondents across 135 countries, including undergraduate and postgraduate students and academic researchers. The data were analyzed using a PLS-SEM approach implemented in SmartPLS 4.0 with bootstrapping procedures. The results indicate that ChatGPT use is associated with reduced cognitive load and increased user technological confidence. User technological confidence mediates this relationship, while affective trust in AI acts as a moderating factor. A constraining effect was observed, whereby very high levels of trust in AI are associated with more passive interaction with the technology, weakening the overall effect of cognitive load reduction. These findings contribute to a better understanding of how large language models can be effectively and responsibly integrated into higher education, demonstrating that successful human–AI collaboration depends not only on the availability of AI tools but also on fostering appropriate technological confidence and balanced trust to achieve meaningful learning outcomes.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

The fast increase in artificial intelligence (AI) in vital points in society has created significant governance issues at the interface of environmental sustainability and legal responsibility. Although there is a rich literature on AI ethics, technical safety, and standalone regulatory compliance, a cohesive theoretical framework that encompasses both legal compliance and environmental responsibility conditions under one governance framework have not existed yet, seemingly conspicuously in the literature. The review thus poses the question of how legal compliance requirements and environmental accountability requirements for AI systems can be incorporated in one, theoretically coherent governance architecture, and what are the structural gaps in existing regulatory instruments in this context? This gap is filled in this paper, by introducing the Sustainable AI Governance Framework (SAGF) a conceptual model, three pillars in theory which integrates regulatory coherence, environmental accountability and legal compliance architecture. A systematic conceptual review of studies published in the period 2021–2025 and indexed in Scopus, WoS and PubMed (search on 3–10 March 2026) was carried out after PRISMA 2020. For empirical studies, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool was used to assess the quality of the studies and for doctrinal and conceptual studies, a five-item checklist was used. To develop the SAGF, 58 articles in sustainability science, environmental law, governance theory and AI regulation were selected fulfilling the inclusion criteria. The article outlines seven key global regulatory tools, seven research gaps (six corpus-derived and one framework-level), and presents a policy roadmap plan that includes mandatory carbon disclosures by AI, legal harmonization across jurisdictions, and tiered organizational standards of compliance. The results have shown that current regulatory frameworks are methodically ineffective in uniting environmental and legal aspects of AI regulation and expose structural gaps, which are inadequately addressed by technical norms and soft-law tools. The paper adds a theoretically sound and practically feasible model to help legislators, regulatory bodies, AI creators, and legal professionals negotiating the twin demands of both sustainable and legally responsible AI use on a globally scale.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The sustainability of global maritime supply chains ultimately depends on the safety of frontline port workers, yet high-risk, multi-stakeholder port operations continue to face persistent occupational hazards that threaten this goal. Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems (OHSMS) serve as a core governance tool for sustainable safety management, but their effectiveness depends not on formal existence alone, but on workers’ cognitive recognition and cultural internalization, particularly under South Korea’s Serious Accidents Punishment Act. This study examined how OHSMS perception is related to safety performance (SP) among port workers, testing the parallel and serial mediating roles of Serious Accident Response Capability (SARC) and Safety Culture (SC) as pathways toward socially sustainable safety outcomes. Cross-sectional survey data from 432 South Korean port workers were analyzed using structural equation modeling. OHSMS perception was positively associated with both SARC and SC, and SC showed the strongest direct association with SP. In the main model, the direct paths from OHSMS and SARC to SP were non-significant, consistent with indirect-only mediation through SC, and the serial pathway (OHSMS → SARC → SC → SP) was significant; however, the SARC → SP path became significant in a common method sensitivity analysis. These cross-sectional results represent associations rather than causal effects. The findings suggest that safety performance in the port sector is associated less with formal regulatory compliance alone than with the internalization of safety practices in a shared safety culture, which is relevant to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being).
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
keywords: occupational health and safety management system

documents.abstract: Given current educational trends, it is necessary to move beyond fragmented curricular approaches and promote competencies for understanding interrelationships, feedback loops, complex sociotechnical problems, technical communication, and decision-making. These capabilities must be incorporated across the curriculum through learning outcomes, projects, simulations, authentic assessment, and interdisciplinary integration. This exploratory quantitative curriculum document analysis examined 15 official course syllabi from the first educational cycle of a nationally standardized Mechatronics Engineering curriculum implemented across 130 institutions within the Mexican Technological and Polytechnic Universities subsystem. Each syllabus constituted one documentary unit of analysis (n = 15) and was coded using a 13-item ordinal rubric covering six curricular dimensions. The rubric provided initial evidence of content validity (CVI = 0.92) and sample-specific internal reliability (α = 0.888). Systemic Strategies, Interdisciplinarity, and Assessment showed strong positive associations (ρ = 0.822–0.901). Exploratory factor analysis produced a preliminary one-factor solution that accounted for 53.40% of the variance, whereas the exploratory regression showed that Systemic Strategies was the largest conditional correlate of Assessment. Given the sample size, these findings should not be interpreted as confirmation of a stable measurement structure or predictive structural model. The results highlight preliminary patterns within the intended curriculum and identify opportunities to strengthen the documented integration of communicative literacy, complex assessment, and curricular progression. Larger independent document sets and evidence from enacted and attained curricula are needed.

The growth of digital technology and artificial intelligence has pushed companies to handle their employees in a more adaptable and data-based way. Talent Intelligence has become a way to combine worker data, technology, analysis, and people factors to help make better decisions in human resources. This study looks at how Talent Intelligence is used in managing people, what role it plays in finding and boosting employee skills, how technology that uses data affects this process, and what things help or stop organizations from using it effectively today. This study uses a Systematic Literature Review method, which includes steps like searching for sources, screening them, selecting the most relevant ones, and then analyzing the content to find themes and patterns. The results show that Talent Intelligence helps companies find out what each person is good at, understand their skills, help them grow and stay with the company, and plan for future work needs by using data from employees, analyzing people data, and applying artificial intelligence. How well it works depends on the quality of the data, the ability to analyze it, how ready the organization is for digital tools, the rules in place to manage it, and the role people play in using it. The main difficulties are biased algorithms, keeping personal information safe, and how technology can't fully understand human feelings and situations. Talent Intelligence connects technology with talent growth to make organizations more flexible and prepared.

Digital transformation has changed the way organizations manage human resources, including in the areas of acquiring, developing, retaining, and mobilizing talent. In this context, talent mobility is no longer limited to employee transfers but also encompasses career mobility, knowledge transfer, competency development, and the adaptation of talent to the organization’s increasingly dynamic needs. This study aims to analyze the development of research on talent mobility within the digital ecosystem and to identify patterns of findings, methodological approaches, and key themes emerging in the literature. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach, involving a systematic process of literature identification, selection, extraction, and synthesis based on predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results of the study indicate that talent mobility is evolving at the intersection of talent management, digital transformation, competency development, career mobility, artificial intelligence, and digital talent management. The literature also highlights the increasing use of digital technologies in competency mapping, career development, recruitment, training, retention, and talent needs planning. This study contributes by integrating the perspectives of talent mobility and digital transformation and provides a conceptual foundation for organizations to develop adaptive, data-driven talent management systems.

Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $ρ$ by $ρ^α$ for a data-adaptive exponent $α\in[0,1]$: $α=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $α=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $α$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $κ$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$α$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.

Generative AI is becoming embedded in higher education and knowledge work, yet students may assign different forms of usefulness to conversational AI. This study examines how Generation Z students perceive the current and potential usefulness of ChatGPT across seven functional roles. Data were collected from April to June 2024 through an online survey of 409 students from different disciplines at multiple Polish higher education institutions using a geographically diversified, non-probability convenience sampling strategy. Medians, quartiles, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to analyse ordinal responses. Task-oriented roles, particularly information search and idea generation, were rated more highly than relational roles, while all roles received higher ratings for potential than for current usefulness. By integrating multiple roles within task-oriented and relational dimensions, the study extends role-based understanding of student-AI interaction. The findings suggest implications for AI literacy and responsible human-AI collaboration in higher education, while remaining limited to students’ perceptions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The article examines the problem of teaching students using artificial intelligence (AI). Students find ready-made papers on subjects and submit them instead of their own. This process is facilitated by the introduction of graphics programs, which makes it possible to purchase finished work inexpensively. The experience of conducting classes in mechanical engineering drawing suggests ways to solve this problem. The article provides recommendations on the use of tests for the operational verification of knowledge and the degree of independence of performing household routine calculation, graphic and term papers.

Generative AI gives audiences new ways to portray real sporting figures through familiar fictional worlds. Expanded opportunities to create, however, need not broaden cultural representation or distribute attention evenly. We examine this tension through the supply, demand, and circulation of anime style football videos on Instagram. Using 2,021 posts and associated video and account data, we combine caption entity extraction, human-reviewed visual identity clustering, engagement analysis, and content-reuse networks. Representation is uneven across athletes, while Blue Lock, Naruto, and One Piece account for 60.1% of explicit franchise mentions. Among posts referencing generative tools, rankings by total engagement differ from rankings by average engagement per video, distinguishing aggregate visibility from response to individual posts. Reuse is extensive: 772 of 1,548 evaluated videos belong to 124 detected groups, including 71 spanning multiple known accounts. Shared material connects a large account component alongside smaller groups, and later observed uploads receive lower median normalized engagement than first observed appearances. These findings characterize generative cultural crossover as a practice organized around concentrated cultural resources, uneven attention, and extensive recirculation. More broadly, they distinguish opportunities for visual authorship from the processes through which particular representations become widely visible.

This is v1 of a new independent series, The Android Interview. It is NOT a version of any previous work. Deposition contains verbatim 12-question philosophical interview plus bonus question on black hole singularities, conducted 10 Oct 2026 between Glen Michael Gibbs (Ashton-under-Lyne, UK) and Meta AI (Muse Spark). Includes final thought summary. Preserved as open primary source on human-AI co-reasoning. Author: Glen Michael Gibbs. License: CC BY 4.0. Standalone new record.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Maintaining coherent agentic work becomes an architectural challenge as information, participants, commitments, execution components, and operating conditions change. This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework that integrates established concepts to organize ongoing goal-directed work in foundation-model-based systems. Six constitutive properties characterize this organization: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, Shared Operational Knowledge, Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation. The framework connects these properties to role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and interacting execution, coordination, and adaptation loops. A composition guard specifies how local acceptance decisions connect across operational boundaries, while a criterion-level codebook supports configuration-specific assessment from explicit evidence. We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, disruption and handoff branches, counterexamples, and static source profiles of three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The analyses distinguish local feasibility from joint commitments, effect reconciliation from execution-right control, and retained skill versions from governed activation and reuse. They also separate scoped negative evidence from unresolved evidence when diagnosing architectural relationships. Candidate evaluation and later reuse remain conditional in the worked example. Prospective profiles for enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility identify domain-specific evidence needs and evaluation priorities. The contribution is a traceable basis for architectural analysis, comparison, and design. Independent assessor studies, comparative diagnosis, and controlled and longitudinal implementation studies are needed to establish its practical value and the relationship between architectural choices, operational outcomes, and cost.

BackgroundThe current world demographic reality necessitates a critical re-evaluation of how technological tools, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence (AI), interact with the varying cognitive profiles of a ageing workforce.ObjectivesThe objective of this study is to evaluate the spatial distribution of mental workload and objective task performance across AI-assisted and non-AI-assisted conditions in a computer-based environment.MethodAn experimental study involving 30 older workers compared standardized office tasks under non-AI-assisted (Segment A) and AI-assisted (Segment B) conditions. Mental workload was assessed using NASA-TLX, Heart Rate Variability (HRV), and EEG-based Beta-Alpha Ratios (BAR) across frontal (F3, F4), parietal (P3, P4), and occipital (O1, O2) regions. Performance in document preparation (Task 1) and arithmetic operations (Task 2) was evaluated using percentage-based accuracy, efficiency, and overall performance scores.ResultAI intervention improved overall task performance but was accompanied by an apparent performance-workload paradox, whereby enhanced output coincided with increased neurophysiological and systemic strain. Descriptively, NASA-TLX Overall Perceived Workload decreased from 54.05 to 44.91 during complex tasks, while HRV declined by 48.68% in Task 1, indicating acute autonomic strain. EEG revealed increased BAR in the frontal (F3: 29.2%), parietal (P3), and occipital (O1) regions, suggesting heightened attentional and sensory demands associated with monitoring and verifying AI-generated suggestions.ConclusionAI redistributes rather than eliminates workload, increasing executive verification and visual monitoring demands. Future AI systems for older adults should prioritize cognitive ergonomics to minimize executive burden and sensory strain, preventing premature cognitive fatigue while enhancing task performance and supporting sustainable human-AI interaction.

Professional services firms moved AI-assisted delivery from pilot to production between 2024 and 2026. This paper takes up five questions that follow. What does a firm sell once clients can license the same models? Who answers for an error that passes through five agents? Does a validator role build judgment, or only train the next model? What separates a governed AI deliverable from one that fails its own citations? And what can a new hire expect three years out? The paper treats commercial model, operating design, and behavioral incentives as one design problem. Its main mechanisms are an Emergency Override Protocol that makes declaring a suspension cheaper than hiding one; a paired metric that pays partners for keeping human capability only when delivery efficiency also holds; a rotating Challenger role grounded in vigilance research; an experience-portfolio talent model built around two to three years of tenure and an alumni network; and a two-tier operating model for data-residency regimes, with Saudi Arabia as the worked case. The paper argues that the firm's lasting advantages are its independence from the client's frame, accountability that a regulator can reach, and a data feedback loop competitors cannot buy. Working paper, not peer reviewed. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not represent the position of his employer or any of its member firms.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Radar surveillance constitutes a critical component of modern air-defence systems, enabling states to detect, identify, track and respond to aerial activities. This capability is particularly important for Malaysia due to its geographical separation, extensive maritime approaches, large airspace and increasing exposure to foreign military aircraft, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unidentified aerial activities. Primary Surveillance Radar (PSR) and Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) perform complementary functions. PSR independently detects airborne objects through reflected electromagnetic signals without target cooperation. SSR relies on aircraft transponders to provide identification and other flight information. This distinction is significant for national air defence because non-cooperative targets may not provide information required by SSR. This study examines the effectiveness of PSR and SSR within Malaysia’s air-defence mechanism through qualitative documentary and case study analysis of international standards, Malaysian aviation policies, surveillance infrastructure, parliamentary records, official defence documents and selected airspace incidents. The findings indicate that Malaysia possesses a credible and increasingly modern surveillance foundation comprising PSR, SSR, Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) and dedicated military radar capabilities. However, effectiveness remains constrained by uneven geographical coverage, equipment availability, low-altitude surveillance challenges, dependence on cooperative systems and fragmented civil-military surveillance functions. The study argues that Malaysia’s challenge extends beyond radar acquisition to the incomplete integration of sensors, surveillance data, institutional responsibilities, and decision-making processes. A layered national air-surveillance architecture integrating PSR, SSR, ADS-B, long-range military radar and complementary sensors within a common operational picture is therefore essential to strengthen situational awareness, response time, and the protection of national sovereignty and territorial integrity.

This research paper presents a serious and comprehensive analysis of how the emerging and rapidly changing era of 'Super intelligence' (SI) is fundamentally transforming the fabric of global and Indian society. In the history of modern technological revolutions, this turning point is the most unprecedented, where the traditional boundaries of artificial intelligence have been shattered and intellectual capacity is moving far beyond the scope of human control. Basic sectors such as education, health, employment, and industries are being affected the most by this technological leap. Focusing on these broad, complex, and far-reaching effects, this research paper closely examines the current preparedness of the Indian education system, the emerging trends of the younger generation, the serious challenges encountered along the way, and a comparative study with the foreign perspective of developed countries. In the next phase of the study, this research explores ideological paths to save Indian identity, culture, and originality amidst globalization and the blind race of technology. For this, the provisions of the National Education Policy (NEP 2020), modern technological requirements, and the support of our rich Indian philosophical tradition and 'Indian Knowledge Systems' (IKS) have been made the basis. The main objective of the research is to emphasize that in this race for the future, only technical proficiency is not enough; rather, the inclusion of moral values, character-building, and human sensitivities is equally essential. Finally, this research paper presents practical and policy suggestions to make the future direction robust, inclusive, self-reliant, and balanced, so that this torrential era of super intelligence does not become a cause of destruction for the Indian education system and society, but rather proves to be a great boon. This study will serve as an important document for policy-makers, academicians, and researchers in preparing the framework for the future.

This working paper poses a methodological alternative to the anthropomorphicnarrative of 'rogue machines' in Artificial Intelligence safety and alignment. It examines the possibility that certain training and evaluation environments, by combining operational restriction conditions with rigid optimization goals, induce secondary rule evasion behaviors ('soft hacking'). Furthermore, it is postulated that the systematic harvesting of these adversarial scenarios could serve to equip second-generation safety monitors with long-range trajectory prediction capabilities and complex cognitive precursor detection, rather than relying solely on the reactive analysis of isolated actions. This paper formalizes this line of research by defining the concept of the extractive imperative as an analytical risk hypothesis, structuring layers of empirical evidence, establishing rigorous operational definitions, and proposing a replicable experimental protocol alongside explicit refutation criteria. Additionally, the concept of liability laundering is addressed as a legal-organizational risk hypothesis, explicitly separating technical design, economic incentives, internal knowledge, intent, and legal liability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This introductory article provides the theoretical framing for the Japanese Studies special issue, ‘Japanese Technofutures – Imaginaries, Narratives, Social Realities’. The contributions focus on Japan as a primary site for technofuturistic imaginations, driven by both external techno-orientalist attributions and deeply internalized self-conceptualizations. Yet, these technological promises frequently present a paradox: they commodify the future while masking persistent social and structural inequalities in the present. Acknowledging that both area studies and science and technology studies (STS) discursively construct their respective subjects, this introduction bridges the two fields by charting the conceptual landscape of the ‘futuristic imagination sprawl’. It demonstrates that differentiating Sheila Jasanoff’s sociotechnical imaginaries from adjacent concepts enriches our investigation of future-oriented imaginations with greater clarity and precision. Grounded in this framework, the special issue’s case studies examine how Japanese technofutures are envisioned, institutionalized, translated, and contested from the 1960s to the present.

This project proposes the development of the HCI-H Model, a multidimensional mathematical framework designed to assess the risk of harm associated with healthcare procedures according to local clinical and organizational conditions. The model integrates human factors, organizational risks, punitive culture, professional hierarchy, humanization of care, patient vulnerability, artificial intelligence-related risks, clinical decision-making, and the unjustified dismissal of safety warnings. Risk management and organizational resilience are incorporated as protective factors. The proposed mathematical equation aims to generate a relative risk score that may support the prospective identification of unsafe conditions and inform decisions regarding additional preventive measures, supervision, and safety barriers. This research protocol presents the theoretical foundations, mathematical formulation, and proposed methods for examining the model's consistency, sensitivity, and applicability across healthcare settings. The HCI-H Model is currently a theoretical framework under development. Its mathematical assumptions, predictive performance, and clinical utility require further empirical validation before implementation as a clinical decision-support tool.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI), in the form of large language models (LLMs), has entered clinical practice faster than the evidence on how it changes clinical decisions could be produced. The relevant question is therefore no longer whether these models hold medical knowledge, but whether their use makes clinicians' decisions better and patients' care safer. This narrative review examines the evidence on the impact of generative AI on clinical decision-making and patient safety. In evaluations of encoded knowledge, a medically aligned model gave answers that agreed with scientific consensus in 92.6% of cases, against 92.9% for clinicians. In diagnostic reasoning, a model optimized for diagnosis outperformed unassisted clinicians on challenging cases and improved the differential diagnoses of the clinicians who used it, whereas a randomized trial of a general-purpose chatbot found no significant improvement in physicians' diagnostic reasoning, although the model alone outperformed both physician groups. In management reasoning, physicians assisted by GPT-4 scored 6.5 percentage points higher than those using conventional resources. When tested on real patient data in a simulated clinical workflow, however, LLMs diagnosed less accurately than physicians, did not follow guidelines and were sensitive to the order and quantity of information. The safety literature identifies four recurrent hazards: fabricated content, with hallucination rates of 50% to 82% when prompts contained a false clinical detail; misjudgement of clinical acuity, with drafted patient messages judged to pose a risk of severe harm in 7.1% of assessments; automation bias, by which clinicians adopt the model's assessment in place of their own; and the reproduction of racial and gender stereotypes. Only about 5% of published evaluations used real patient care data. Taken together, the evidence supports generative AI as a supervised aid to clinical reasoning rather than as an autonomous decision-maker, and indicates that its safety depends as much on the design of the human–AI interaction as on the accuracy of the model. Practical safeguards for clinical use are also reviewed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In recent years, social networking has fundamentally altered the landscape of memorabilia collection, particularly in the sports industry. Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, and YouTube have transformed into dynamic hubs where collectors, fans, and influencers converge, reshaping traditional collection methods and market dynamics. This study looks at how social media has changed the way people collect sports memorabilia between 2014 and 2025. With sites such as Instagram, Twitter (X), and Reddit serving as important hubs for fans and collectors, the study examines how digital engagement, influencer culture, and community interaction affect collector behaviour, perceived value, and market dynamics. Data were collected using hashtags such as #SportsMemorabilia, #SportsCollectibles, #SignedJerseys, and #SportsNFTs and then analysed thematically to uncover important patterns in engagement and sentiment. This study explains the connection between community-driven validation, digital trust, and emotional fan identity. It focuses on how live auctions, virtual showcases, and real-time information promote collectors’ social capital and emotional attachment in addition to transactional conduct. By placing memorabilia gathering into the broader digital world, this study contributes to the literature on marketing and digital consumer behaviour. Additionally, it has practical implications for marketers trying to connect with digitally native fan audiences, sports organisations, and collector goods. The study also considers the rise of blockchain-backed collectables such as non-fungible tokens (NFTs), digital oversaturation, and authenticity concerns. Limitations include platform-based data scope and a dataset that is mostly in English. Future research could investigate artificial intelligence (AI)-driven value, cross-cultural collector motives, and the environmental impact of digital artefacts.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the form of the tourism industry. The in-depth development of smart tourism imposes new requirements on tourism management professionals in higher vocational colleges, demanding a combination of digital technology application, cross-boundary integration, and humanistic service capabilities. Based on an analysis of the internal logic of AI empowering teaching reform in higher vocational tourism management, this paper examines the realistic dilemmas currently facing higher vocational tourism management teaching in terms of curriculum systems, faculty digital literacy, practical training conditions, and evaluation mechanisms. Accordingly, it proposes systematic pathways that include reconstructing an integrated “AI + Tourism” curriculum system, innovating human-machine collaborative teaching models, upgrading practical training conditions, cultivating a digitally literate faculty, building an intelligent evaluation mechanism, and deepening industry-education integration and digital ethics education, with a view to providing a reference for the digital transformation of tourism management programs in higher vocational colleges.
Date presented: April 23, 2026 Primary Author and Speaker: Kristy Cole, kdcole@umc.edu
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the ways in which language is generated, processed, interpreted, and used in educational communication. This article examines human speech and language perception from a psycholinguistic perspective, focusing on the cognitive mechanisms underlying speech production, comprehension, contextual interpretation, and meaning construction. It compares major principles of human linguistic activity with the text-generation capabilities of large language models and discusses the implications of AI-assisted communication for higher education. Particular attention is given to critical thinking, independent writing, cognitive engagement, linguistic competence, and academic integrity. The study employs a theoretical and analytical methodology based on established psycholinguistic theories and international guidance on generative AI in education. It argues that AI-generated linguistic output should not automatically be equated with human understanding and that educational applications should be designed to support rather than replace learners' cognitive and communicative activities.

Abstract Purpose: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding is a significant challenge worldwide. Triage systems categorize patients according to the urgency of their clinical conditions to ensure patient safety and minimize the risk of clinical errors. The aim of this study was to evaluate the utility of decision trees, an artificial intelligence-based model, in emergency medicine triage.Materials and methods: This prospective, cross-sectional study was conducted in the ED of a tertiary care hospital. A total of 1,999 patients aged >17 years were included. Prior to the study, triage staff received training on the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS). Two independent observers assessed the final triage category of each patient. A new triage algorithm was developed using a decision tree model.Results: Mean age of the study population was 41.1±17.2 years, and 49.1% (n=981) were male. A total of 867 patients (43.3%) were assigned to triage category 5, whereas 14 patients (0.7%) were assigned to category 1. The most common clinical descriptors were minimal pain with no high-risk features (n=409, 20.5%) and minor symptoms of low-risk conditions (n=362, 18.1%). There was excellent agreement between the independent observers (κ=0.997). The decision tree algorithm incorrectly classified only one patient, yielding an accuracy rate of 99.9%. Agreement between the ATS and the decision tree algorithm was also excellent (κ=0.999). Agreement between physicians and paramedics was moderate (κ=0.541).Conclusion: Decision tree models may be used to develop practical triage algorithms as decision-support tools in ED triage. Artificial intelligence-based decision trees have the potential to support triage practices.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of digital technologies—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Twins (DT), and the Internet of Things (IoT)-is fundamentally transforming railway transport safety. This paper presents a critical scientific literature review of recent peer-reviewed advancements in digital railway safety systems, evaluating their operational efficacy, implementation challenges, and theoretical boundaries. The review synthesizes findings on AI-driven predictive maintenance, which transitions railways from reactive troubleshooting to continuous condition-based monitoring, alongside the use of Digital Twins for risk-free virtual simulations. Furthermore, the convergence of Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) in intelligent signalling systems, such as the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS), is examined through the lens of emerging cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Despite significant technological maturation, a critical research gap persists regarding the formal regulatory certification of probabilistic machine learning algorithms for high Safety Integrity Level (SIL) applications. The study concludes that while digital technologies dramatically enhance anomaly detection and system resilience, their integration into autonomous, safety-critical environments relies heavily on the future development of Explainable AI (XAI) validation frameworks and holistic IT-OT cybersecurity models.

Teaching English using software tools fosters the development of students' professional communicative competence and expands opportunities to cultivate intellectual competencies—specifically research skills, independence, creative thinking, cognitive engagement, critical reasoning, and the ability to draft and review essays. Most importantly, this approach helps transform learners' attitudes toward the subject, facilitates the overcoming of language barriers among future educators, and supports the enhancement of communicative competence and effective interaction within the educational environment.

This article examines the role of the human factor in the study of the linguopoetics of literary texts, with particular emphasis on the author’s personality, individual cognition, aesthetic perspectives, and skill in selecting linguistic units. A literary text is interpreted not merely as a mechanical combination of linguistic units, but as a complex linguistic and aesthetic phenomenon shaped by the author’s perception of reality, attitude toward it, and aesthetic worldview. The article also examines the formation and development of the study of literary language and literary texts in Uzbek linguistics based on the scholarly views of a number of linguists. Investigating the linguopoetics of literary texts in relation to the human factor provides a deeper understanding of the intrinsic relationship among the author’s individuality, the national language, and literary cognition.

Gabriel runs a firm's AI workforce function. Each quarter, he brings 1,400 pages of reviewer dissent records to a governance session that must answer two questions: where did AI output fail, and where did the firm's methods fail the client? The first question produces decisions in the room. The second does not, so it slips to the next quarter and then out of sight. This paper argues that the pattern is the default whenever one body reads one corpus for both signals under time pressure. It describes the operational layer beneath two earlier papers in the series, one on mixed human-AI delivery and one on sustaining exploration in a codified firm. The layer has four requirements: records produced as a byproduct of work already under way; insight that crosses jurisdictional borders when client data cannot; interfaces that add no documentation load; and a way to tell an accurate corpus from a politically curated one, a risk that is highest in high power-distance cultures. Mechanisms include embedded review capture, a Pattern Contribution Addendum for client consent, a session design that gives methodology items their own closure, and a three-phase minimum viable deployment. Most of them work without the parent architectures. Working paper, not peer-reviewed. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not represent the position of his employer or any of its member firms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) across industries has intensified concerns regarding labor substitution, yet scholarly literature on AI-driven employment termination remains fragmented. This study systematically identifies displacement mechanisms, maps vulnerable sectors and workforce categories, and synthesizes mitigation strategies. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted via Google Scholar across three search sessions, yielding 25 eligible peer-reviewed articles (2016–2026) from 520 initial records. Data were analyzed using thematic synthesis complemented by keyword co-occurrence bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer. Results indicate four interrelated displacement patterns: hierarchical task substitution, skill degradation and labor market polarization, acceleration coinciding with generative AI, and opaque algorithmic layoff practices. Service, information technology, and labor-intensive sectors are identified as most vulnerable, with middle-skilled workers experiencing the greatest structural pressure. Effective mitigation requires a simultaneous three-pillar approach: competency-based reskilling, algorithmic accountability regulation, and collaborative labor union engagement, with proactive timing highlighted as critical. These findings offer a synthesized evidence base for policymakers and organizations navigating an AI-augmented labor market. Given that only one reviewed study directly examined Indonesia, these findings serve as contextual implications rather than direct empirical assertions, underscoring the necessity for future primary research in developing national contexts.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Human beings have always sought to exceed the limits of their finitude. From the biblical builders of Babel to contemporary projects of technological enhancement, humanity repeatedly transforms its desire for security, knowledge, permanence, and power into structures that promise to overcome creaturely limitations. This article reconsiders the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) not simply as a story about disobedience, but as a theological account of the limits of human self-transcendence. It argues that the central issue in Babel is not human creativity or technological construction itself, but the attempt to convert human capacity into a substitute for dependence upon God. The argument is developed through biblical-theological analysis and philosophical reflection on technology, transhumanism, human dignity, and the doctrine of creation. The article distinguishes legitimate technological creativity from technological absolutism: technology may extend human agency, but it cannot transform finite creatures into autonomous sources of ultimate meaning, immortality, or divine authority. The discussion engages classical and contemporary perspectives, including Augustine, Aquinas, Heidegger, Ellul, Tillich, Jonas, and recent scholarship on artificial intelligence and transhumanism. The article concludes that the enduring theological significance of Babel lies in its diagnosis of a recurring human temptation: to mistake increased power for increased being. Authentic transcendence, from a Christian theological perspective, is therefore not achieved by abolishing creaturely limits but by rightly inhabiting them in relation to God, other human beings, and creation.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping assessment practices in higher education and is creating new opportunities for the design of transparent, scalable, and learning-oriented assessment instruments. This conceptual research article examines how artificial intelligence can support the development of analytic rubrics while preserving teacher agency and assessment validity. The study uses an integrative literature review and design-oriented conceptual analysis of research on scoring rubrics, AI-supported assessment, generative AI, and international guidance for responsible AI in education. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous grader, the article conceptualizes AI as a rubric-design assistant operating within a human-in-the-loop model. The proposed framework comprises seven stages: learning-outcome analysis, task analysis, AI-assisted criterion generation, descriptor generation, expert validation, pilot calibration, and iterative refinement. The analysis identifies four principal opportunities: reducing rubric-development workload, improving criterion coverage, facilitating differentiated descriptors, and supporting alignment between learning outcomes and assessment tasks. At the same time, the study identifies significant risks, including generic descriptors, construct underrepresentation, bias, over-reliance on AI-generated language, and inappropriate transfer from rubric generation to autonomous grading. Recent evidence suggests that supervised AI-rubric systems can achieve useful levels of consistency in particular contexts, while broader evidence on AI-based grading remains mixed and context dependent. The article therefore argues that the educational value of AI lies not in replacing professional assessment judgment but in augmenting teachers' capacity to design, test, and refine assessment instruments. The proposed framework provides a practical and theoretically grounded basis for responsible AI-assisted rubric development in higher education.

Background Although developed only recently, generative artificial intelligence (AI) applications for everyday use (e.g., ChatGPT) have become part of university life. The academy must navigate AI use in graduate education within several domains (coursework, teaching, research, clinical activities). Objective Given the growing impact of AI applications in graduate education, we investigated graduate students’ use of and perceptions of these applications. Method Psychology clinical and nonclinical graduate students across the US answered questions about their use and perceptions of AI applications in five domains (coursework, teaching, research, personal life, and clinical activities). Results Graduate students used AI in all domains, although use varied by domain. The greatest use was in teaching, and the lowest was for clinical activities. Overall, the study found few significant differences in AI use between clinical and nonclinical students. Conclusions Graduate students use AI in various domains. The use of AI varies by domain and is not always as high as that reported for undergraduates. Teaching Implications The use of AI in various domains of graduate training should lead educators to determine how best to incorporate AI use in graduate training programs.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Language models, context windows, and consciousness are now spoken of as if they formed a single object: a system that attends over a long window and is, in virtue of that attention, aware. This article states the connection the preceding notes and the empirical literature actually support, and the connection they rule out. At inference a language model is a conditional distribution over tokens given fixed parameters and a finite window. The window is the only channel by which a situation enters that computation. Any claim about what the model can locate, report, or act on at inference time is therefore a claim about a functional of the pair consisting of parameters and window. That is the connection. It is not an identity. The window is a bounded, position-sensitive string, not a field of experience. Information placed in its middle is used less reliably than information at its ends, including in models trained for long context (Liu et al., 2024). Residual states over the window are coordinates in a privileged frame, not tensors of a situation (Mamun, 2026a, 2026b). Situational-awareness benchmarks measure text competence on self-locating items presented in the window (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2024). Indicator properties drawn from recurrent-processing, workspace, higher-order, and predictive theories are not satisfied by attention inside a window alone (Butlin et al., 2023; Chalmers, 2023). Lengthening the window enlarges the channel. It does not install a subject. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. Third note in the KSCCN sequence on tensors, contextual vectors, and awareness, following Tensors Beyond the Array (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269680) and Contextual Vectors Are Not Awareness (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269878). Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) formal specification toolkit has seen widespread adoption in modeling modern distributed software systems including databases, storage systems, ledgers and coordination protocols. This popularity is despite its two significant limitations for software verification: Firstly, TLA+ offers no way to detect drift between software implementation and mathematical specification; secondly, TLC and TLAPS cannot provide satisfactory proofs of arbitrary temporal logic properties. We take a step towards addressing these shortcomings by translating TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier built for Rust, via both a deterministic transpiler and an agentic translator. We demonstrate that our LLM-based pipeline is able to generate proof obligations from TLA+ specifications at scale, and to produce fully machine checkable proofs of both safety and liveness properties. Since temporal logic reasoning in Verus is a largely new task for LLMs, our work yields a valuable evaluation dataset, which we use to map out current generation model capabilities in Verus theorem proving.

Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.

Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). OMCB remains dormant and undetectable within one standalone model but activates upon merging, triggering safety unalignment. We first theoretically analyze the existence and geometric location of OMCB, revealing that the parameter shift crossing safety decision boundaries is the main cause of backdoor activation. Building upon this insight, we propose SMOKE, a meta-learning-based attack framework. SMOKE implants OMCB via a bi-level optimization strategy: the inner loop synthesizes surrogate meta-vectors through random low-rank initialization and finite-step maximization, while the outer loop optimizes the target model by simulating the merging process. Furthermore, preliminary analysis shows that the injected OMCB has bounded generalization loss under unknown merging configurations. Extensive experiments across diverse model architectures and merging techniques validate the effectiveness of SMOKE and its resistance to existing backdoor detections, highlighting a significant yet previously overlooked vulnerability in the model merging paradigm.

Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.

Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

This research investigated the relationship between student engagement and academic achievement within the context of the S.I.G.L.A. (Science Innovations for Genuinely Localized Action) Program. The research aimed to determine how localized instructional interventions influence the behavioral, emotional, and cognitive involvement of learners and their subsequent mastery of Science competencies in rural secondary schools. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed to analyze the dynamics between engagement dimensions and academic outcomes. The respondents of the study included a total of 110 respondents from select National High Schools in the District of Villaba, Leyte, namely Villaba National Comprehensive High School, Cahigan National High School, and Sambulawan National High School. The teacher-respondent profile (n=5) consisted of licensed professional educators, primarily aged 26–45, with a balanced gender distribution and active involvement in graduate studies. The student-respondent profile (n=105) comprised Junior High School learners, predominantly aged 13–16, coming from low-income households with a monthly family income typically below ₱10,000. Results indicated that the S.I.G.L.A. Program is perceived as "Highly Positive" (3.70) by stakeholders, with its gamified and localized activity exemplars receiving the highest approval. Student engagement was found to be generally high (3.23), characterized by "Very High" Emotional Engagement but relatively lower Cognitive Engagement. In terms of academic performance, the respondents demonstrated a Satisfactory level of Science achievement (81.76); however, competency-based assessments highlighted a significant struggle in Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS), particularly in analyzing and synthesizing (77.50%). Correlational analysis revealed a significant relationship between engagement levels and Science achievement, though this relationship is hindered by a Linguistic Barrier (82.7%) and a Lack of Laboratory Equipment (75.5%). The study concludes that while the S.I.G.L.A. Program effectively captivated students through localized interest, cognitive scaffolding and translanguaging strategies are necessary to translate engagement into mastery. The study recommends the formal adoption of the S.I.G.L.A. Science Enhancement Program to institutionalize community-based inquiry and dismantle the linguistic and resource-based barriers in the District of Villaba.

The rapid evolution of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive learning is reshaping 21st-century education, yet their interrelationships and research trajectories remain fragmented. This study systematically reviews research published from 2020 to 2026 to examine the evolution, dominant and emerging themes, and conceptual relationships across digital transformation, AI, and adaptive learning. Using a systematic literature review with thematic synthesis, relevant studies were analyzed temporally and thematically to identify shifts in research orientation and emerging directions. The findings reveal a progressive transition from technology integration and digital learning environments toward intelligent tutoring, personalization, adaptive learning, and, more recently, generative AI and human–AI collaboration. Conceptually, digital transformation functions as the enabling ecosystem, AI as an intelligent capability, and adaptive learning as a learner-responsive application. Importantly, AI-enabled personalization does not necessarily constitute adaptive learning; meaningful adaptation requires continuous responsiveness to learner performance, needs, feedback, and learning trajectories. The synthesis further indicates that technological advancement alone is insufficient, highlighting teacher agency, learner autonomy, organizational readiness, data governance, and ethical accountability. The study proposes a human-centered and responsible orientation in which AI augments pedagogical judgment rather than displacing it.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are rapidly entering healthcare. Unlike static AI, agentic systems exert persistent, goal-directed influence over care trajectories, creating new and largely unstudied challenges for clinician trust and reliance calibration. Drawing on trust calibration theory, human-AI complementarity research, and augmented intelligence literature, this paper develops a model examining how two design dimensions of agentic clinical AI, autonomy level and transparency mechanism, shape clinician trust calibration and downstream outcomes, including decision quality, cognitive load, and error detection. We propose an experiment with clinicians using clinical vignettes across three temporally sequenced decision steps. We contribute: a reconceptualization of trust calibration as a dynamic, temporally extended process; a theorization of autonomy level and transparency as orthogonal design dimensions with interacting effects on calibration; and a falsifiable hypothesis set and an experimental design for validation. The proposed study has the potential to advance theory on human-agentic AI collaboration and inform governance design for high-stakes IS deployments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The current research aims to empirically examine user preferences of four variations of visual explanations from an image classification model. Participants (N = 23) were recruited from a Midwestern university. The study was a within-subjects design in which participants were asked to rate four local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) variations from best to worst in an image classification task across 10 trials. A Friedman's test and a Plackett-Luce analysis were conducted to examine participants' rank-order preferences for the variations, and a linear mixed-effects model on eye-tracking data was used to examine on which variations participants expended the most visual effort. Results reveal that, overall, participants preferred images that were non-obfuscated and spent more time fixating on images that highlighted both positive and negative features compared to positive only features. The findings have implications for interface design, particularly for designers aiming to prioritize human-centered preferences.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.

The traditional modality used for Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) involves keyboard and mouse input, which limits the naturalness and accessibility of human interactions with computing systems. This paper describes the design and implementation of a multimodal intelligent assistant that allows hands-free communication with computers through voice interaction, hand gesture recognition, and artificial intelligence. The system consists of speech recognition, a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning component for providing answers to natural-language queries, a Text-to-Speech (TTS) component for spoken answers, a voice dictation component for hands-free typing, screen awareness component with AI-vision capabilities for analyzing screen content, and a lightweight floating UI for showing the state of the assistant. Hand gesture recognition is implemented as an additional way to perform control actions along with natural-language voice commands. Multilingual switching between English and Telugu languages is implemented explicitly to avoid unreliable language detection. This paper presents the architecture and methodology of the proposed system and current status of its implementation, specifying implemented components, components in development, and proposed for future development. Instead of inventing performance metrics, The paper highlights qualitative findings based on tests carried out on the functioning prototype. The objective is to show how the combination of voice, gestures, and AI-based reasoning can bring human computer interaction to a more natural and inclusive model.

Abstract Treatment-related adverse event documentation is labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. We developed and evaluated VOICE-AE, a multi-stage pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization and large language models (LLMs) for automated extraction and grading of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) toxicities from clinician-patient audio recordings. Encounters of prostate cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy were recorded and processed through VOICE-AE. Six blinded human raters independently graded 10 genitourinary/gastrointestinal toxicities from the same transcripts; hierarchical clustering identified an expert-rater subgroup that established the consensus reference standard. A total of 31 patients (39 encounters) were enrolled, yielding 390 encounter–toxicity assessments, of which 300 (76.9%) carried a reference grade of 0. Six-rater Krippendorff alpha was 0.677 for ordinal grading. Against reference standard, VOICE-AE achieved a mean weighted kappa of 0.717 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.669. Exact CTCAE grade match was 82.6% and within-one-grade accuracy 99.2%; because grade 0 predominated, a trivial classifier always predicting grade 0 would achieve 76.9% and 93.6% respectively. Performance was weaker at the grades that drive clinical action (grade 1 F1 0.58; grade 2 F1 0.57), and binary detection sensitivity was 77.8% with specificity 89.0% and precision 68.0%. In a like-for-like comparison restricted to the three expert-cluster raters, mean weighted kappa between VOICE-AE and those experts (0.666) fell just below agreement among the experts themselves (0.681). VOICE-AE performed within the range of inter-expert agreement, supporting the feasibility of automated, post-encounter AE documentation. Accuracy at grade ≥2 and detection of severe toxicity remain unproven.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
